title: Sending Students To The Office Will Weaken Your Ability To Manage Your Classroom your-ability-to-manage-your-classroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin discloses that in nearly twenty years of teaching he has never sent a student to the office for a behavior issue, framing this not as a boast but as evidence for his argument that doing so weakens a teacher's authority. He carves out a narrow exception for dangerous or grossly insubordinate behavior -- fights, threats, or weapons -- which must involve an administrator and be documented, while insisting all other behavior issues belong solely with the classroom teacher. He argues that sending a student to the office communicates to the class that the teacher lacks full command of the room, eroding both the teacher's confidence and students' perception of the teacher as the final authority. He also questions the practical value of office referrals, noting that busy principals can typically offer only stern lectures or delayed consequences, which are weaker tools than a teacher's immediate, consistent enforcement of a classroom management plan. He distinguishes the 'authoritative' style he advocates, which earns respect, from an 'authoritarian' style that produces resentment, tying the piece back to his broader philosophy expressed in his book Dream Class.
points: The author states he has never sent a student to the office for a behavior issue in nearly twenty years of teaching, using this as evidence for his broader argument.
A narrow exception is carved out for dangerous or grossly insubordinate behavior (fights, threats, weapons), which must be documented and involve an administrator.
Sending students to the office signals to the class that a teacher lacks command of the room, weakening both teacher confidence and student respect.
Busy principals typically can only offer stern lectures or delayed consequences, which are weaker behavior-management tools than a teacher's own immediate, consistent enforcement.
The recommended 'authoritative' style -- firm but respect-earning -- is explicitly distinguished from a resentment-producing 'authoritarian' style of classroom management.
quotes: In nearly 20 years of teaching, I’ve never sent one of my students to the office because of a behavior issue.
It is simply a byproduct of my strong belief that every time you send a student to someone else for a behavior issue (i.e., the principal, vice-principal, or counselor), you weaken your authority.
Witnessing a fight, being challenged and cursed at, and learning a student has brought a weapon to school are all examples of behavior that must be overseen by an administrator.
Every time you send a student to the office, you’re communicating to your students that you don’t have full command of your classroom.

Principals are too busy to monitor students placed in time-out around the office, so they must rely on stern lectures and assurance from the student that the behavior will change. Both are weak methods of behavior management.

It’s important to note, however, that it is an authority that engenders respect (i.e., an authoritative style), not resentment, which is often produced from an authoritarian style of classroom management.
